title: ‘Avengers’ Studio AGBO’s Chris Brearton, Dominic Hughes to Keynote Tokyo Market on Artist-Led AI in Storytelling
description: TIFFCOM, the content market held in coordination with the Tokyo International Film Festival, will host a keynote presentation by Chris Brearton and
body:
TIFFCOM, the content market held in coordination with the Tokyo International Film Festival, will host a keynote presentation by Chris Brearton and Dominic Hughes, partner and chief scientific Officer, respectively, of AGBO, the studio founded by Anthony and Joe Russo. 

	The session, titled “Technology and Storytelling,” takes place Oct. 29 and will be moderated by Naman Ramachandran, Asia editor at Variety.


	Their conversation will focus on how artists, working alongside technologists, can use AI, machine learning and other tools to advance storytelling.
	

	Before joining AGBO, Brearton was VP of corporate strategy at Amazon MGM Studios, where he oversaw the integration of MGM into Amazon. Hughes, a leader in algorithms, machine learning and AI, partners with AGBO’s storytelling and innovation teams to guide the development and deployment of AI technologies within the creative process.

	The Russo Brothers and AGBO have generated more than $7 billion at the global box office and produced 17 No. 1 worldwide debuts, including “Avengers: Endgame.” The studio is currently in post-production on “Avengers: Doomsday,” set for release Dec. 18.

	The keynote leads TIFFCOM’s second wave of confirmed conferences. The Association of Japanese Animations will present a special session on “Japanese Animation’s Global Expansion” on Oct. 30, unveiling the first public data from its 2025 industry survey alongside overseas strategy presentations from Nippon Animation and Production I.G. Speakers include Nippon Animation international sales director Hitomi Hiratsuka and Production I.G. corporate administration and IP director Yoko Ueda, with opening remarks from Association of Japanese Animations president Kazuko Ishikawa.
	

	A co-production conference, “Anime’s New Frontier: Structuring and Financing International Co-Productions,” runs Oct. 29 and features Ervin Han, director of the Annecy-winning “The Violinist” and co-founder of Robot Playground Media, alongside Salamander CEO Taiki Sakurai and Foliascope CEO Ilan Urroz.

	TIFFCOM’s Asian series and film sessions include a showcase of Linmon Pictures’ 2026-2027 drama slate on Oct. 28 and a Taiwan originals project showcase from the Taiwan Drama Production Industry Federation the same day. A “Japan’s IP Frontier” session on Oct. 29 will spotlight six companies, including TV Tokyo, Fuji Television and Hokkaido Television Broadcasting, expanding formats and IP overseas, while Nippon TV and Tokyo Broadcasting System Holdings will each present separate sessions on their global strategies on Oct. 28 and Oct. 29.

	The Tokyo IP Market also welcomes two new participants, digital comics publisher Comisma and toy company Takaratomy, bringing its total to 10 IP holders alongside Amuse Creative Studio, Kadokawa, Nihon Bungeisha, Nippon Animation, Shochiku, Shufu to Seikatsu Sha, Square Enix and Toei.

	TIFFCOM 2026 runs Oct. 28-30 at the Tokyo Metropolitan Industrial Trade Center Hamamatsucho-kan, alongside the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival, which runs Oct. 26-Nov. 4.

schema.headline: ‘Avengers’ Studio AGBO’s Chris Brearton, Dominic Hughes to Keynote Tokyo Market on Artist-Led AI in Storytelling

title: ‘South Park’ Season 29 Premiere Embraces ‘South America’ Name Change With New Theme Song and a Trump Cameo
description: “South Park” — or rather “South America” — made its Season 29 debut Wednesday night and wasted no time introducing audiences to the newly named town
body:
“South Park” — or rather “South America” — made its Season 29 debut Wednesday night and wasted no time introducing audiences to the newly named town.

	The episode, titled “South American Biker Gangs,” kicked off with an updated theme song ringing in the name change — “I’m goin’ down to South America, have myself a time!” — before showing another new addition: a Donald Trump cameo.


	The premiere episode centered around the usual suspects, Cartman, Stan, Kyle and Kenny, and their newfound love of e-bikes. But when the gaggle of kids takes to the streets with their motorized bikes, the parents of South America form their own biker gang in opposition.
	

	As per usual, Kenny dies when his e-bike blows up, and his death unites the town to come together, outlaw e-bikes and begin selling “South America Strong” T-shirts.

	Earlier this month, ahead of the Season 29 premiere, creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone announced that the long-running comedy series would furthermore be known as “South America,” a comedic jab at Trump’s recent moves to rename the likes of Lake Ontario as Lake America, New Mexico as New America and the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.

	“Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of ‘South Park’ to ‘South America,’” the pair shared in a statement. “We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount — a Skydance Capitulation.”

	The show took home the gold for outstanding animated program at the 2026 Creative Arts Emmys, and while celebrating the win, threw another dig at Trump by sharing a graphic of the president with his pants and underwear around his ankles to the official “South Park” X account.
	

	The moves are a continuation of the show’s Season 28 political antics, which included plot points like JD Vance seducing Donald Trump in order to dodge punishment for trying to kill his unborn baby with Satan and Pete Hegseth trying to bust Peter Thiel out of jail.

schema.headline: ‘South Park’ Season 29 Premiere Embraces ‘South America’ Name Change With New Theme Song and a Trump Cameo

title: Virender Sehwag’s ‘Rise & Fall’ Season 2 Sets September Launch on Prime Video, Reveals First Four Contestants (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Virender Sehwag-hosted reality series “Rise & Fall Season 2” is heading to Prime Video this September, with the first four of 15 contestants set to
body:
Virender Sehwag-hosted reality series “Rise & Fall Season 2” is heading to Prime Video this September, with the first four of 15 contestants set to compete across the 42-day run confirmed.

	The Banijay Asia production will be available free of charge on Prime Video and the MX Player Android app – the latter now operating under its refreshed identity as MX Player by Prime Video – with new episodes releasing daily. The four names confirmed are Swara Bhasker, Shehzad Poonawalla, Priyanka Chahar Choudhary and Karan Patel, with the remaining 11 yet to be announced.
	

	The series, adapted from the hit U.K. format originally created by Studio Lambert, is built around a shifting hierarchy in which players move between Ruler and Worker positions, with their standing shaped by in-game decisions rather than scripted outcomes.


	Chahar Choudhary, who has prior reality-television credits, said: “I’ve experienced reality television in different forms, but ‘Rise & Fall Season 2’ brings a whole new dimension to the game. The idea of going from being a Ruler to a Worker and having your position shaped by the choices you make, makes this experience especially exciting for me. Reality shows have taught me to trust my instincts, stay true to myself and play every moment as it comes, but this time, the power dynamics add an entirely different layer. I’m ready to step into the game, take on whatever position comes my way and see how far I can rise.”

	Bhasker said: “I’ve always been someone who wears her opinions on her sleeve, so entering a game like ‘Rise & Fall Season 2’ is going to be quite an experience. The show brings together personalities with very different perspectives, and when power and strategy come into play, I’m sure those differences will make for some fascinating dynamics. I’m excited to see how it all unfolds.”
	

	Patel, known for a long run in Indian television drama, said: “People have seen me play different characters and tell stories through television all these years, but ‘Rise & Fall Season 2’ gives me the chance to enter a completely different arena as myself. What excites me is the competitive side of it having to make a move, back your decision and keep pushing yourself when the game shifts. I’m looking forward to embracing that challenge and giving this game everything I’ve got.”

	Poonawalla added: “My life and journey has been synonymous with rise and fall. Literally this show espouses my journey and even as one chapter ends – a new chapter in life begins with its own set of challenges and opportunities. ‘Rise & Fall Season 2’ feels like a particularly interesting innings for me. I’ve always enjoyed spaces where there is room for a strong point of view and this game brings together people with very different perspectives and ways of looking at things but they must know by now I have zero tolerance for those who try to belittle Bharat and its history. It will be interesting to see how absolute strangers walk into a situation where they have to ally at times or be on opposite sides at other times. On a lighter note – I’m glad I don’t have to pay rent for the next six weeks.”

	“Rise & Fall Season 2” streams free from Sept. 26 on Prime Video and the MX Player Android app.

schema.headline: Virender Sehwag’s ‘Rise & Fall’ Season 2 Sets September Launch on Prime Video, Reveals First Four Contestants (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Zhang Yimou to Lead Busan Competition Jury
description: The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has confirmed seven jurors for its Competition section, with Chinese director Zhang Yimou serving
body:
The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has confirmed seven jurors for its Competition section, with Chinese director Zhang Yimou serving as jury president for the section’s second edition.

	Zhang has won prizes at each of the three major European festivals: the Golden Bear at Berlin for his 1987 debut “Red Sorghum,” the Golden Lion at Venice twice, for “The Story of Qiu Ju” (1992) and “Not One Less” (1999), and the Grand Prix of the Jury at Cannes for “To Live” (1994). His films have also picked up three Academy Award nominations and five Golden Globe nominations. He directed the opening and closing ceremonies for both the 2008 Beijing Summer Olympics and the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics, and remains active with recent work including “One Second” (2021) and “Full River Red” (2023), plus an upcoming adaptation of “The Three-Body Problem.” His history with Busan dates to 2010, when “Under the Hawthorn Tree” opened the festival.
	

	Joining him on the jury is Bi Gan, whose “Resurrection” (2025) played in BIFF’s first Competition last year and won the Artistic Contribution prize; his earlier features “Kaili Blues” (2015) and “Long Day’s Journey Into Night” (2018) drew wide critical notice, the latter premiering in Un Certain Regard at Cannes. Actor Moon Choi, who has moved into directing and producing alongside her acting career, won Actor of the Year at BIFF in 2018 for “Our Body” and stars in and produced this year’s “Bedford Park.” Japanese director Ishikawa Kei, a graduate of Poland’s Łódź Film School, saw his debut “Gukoroku – Traces of Sin” (2016) screen at Venice, while “A Man” (2022) returned to Busan as closing film after its own Venice run and picked up eight Japan Academy Film Prizes.
	

	Rounding out the jury are July Jung, Tran Thi Bich Ngoc and Samal Yeslyamova. Jung became the first South Korean woman director to have all three of her features invited to Cannes, with “A Girl at My Door” (2014) and “Next Sohee” (2022) both playing there before “Dora” (2026), which is also part of this year’s BIFF lineup. Tran, a Vietnamese producer with three decades in the industry, has backed films including “Big Father, Small Father and Other Stories” (2015) and “The Third Wife” (2018), and now runs the project market and DANAFF Talents program at the Danang Asian Film Festival. Yeslyamova, a Kazakhstani actor, won best actress at Cannes for “Ayka” (2018) and has a long history with BIFF, including a stint on its New Currents jury and a role in 2019 opening film “The Horse Thieves. Roads of Time.”

	The jury will evaluate 13 films in this year’s Competition lineup. The Busan Award, presented across five categories, best film, best director, special jury prize, best actor and artistic contribution, carries total prize money of KRW110 million($80,350). Following BIFF’s recognition this year as a FIAPF A-list festival, alongside Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Sundance and Toronto, the best film winner now also qualifies directly for the best international feature film category at the Academy Awards.

	The 31st Busan International Film Festival will Oct. 6-15, at the Busan Cinema Center and throughout Busan, with the 21st Asian Contents & Film Market held Oct. 10-13.

schema.headline: Zhang Yimou to Lead Busan Competition Jury

title: Benjamin Netanyahu Calls to ‘Revoke the Citizenship’ of ‘Anyone Who Slanders IDF Soldiers’ Following ‘NAZA’ Documentary Premiere
description: Following the premiere of “NAZA” at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is calling for the intro
body:
Following the premiere of “NAZA” at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is calling for the introduction of a law that would “revoke the citizenship of anyone who slanders IDF [Israeli Defense Forces] soldiers.”

	“We will hit them in their pockets and also in their citizenship, because their place is not among us,” he said in a video posted to X on Wednesday. He went on to describe another law that would raise “the defamation damages they can be sued for twentyfold.”
	

	“NAZA,” co-directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, who are both Israeli citizens, shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to its official logline. The film features interviews with 24 Israeli military intelligence officers and soldiers.


	The documentary won the special jury prize at the festival, and also received a 24.5-minute standing ovation — the longest in the festival’s history. 

	Netanyahu’s statement comes following the words of Israel’s Minister of Culture Miki Zohar, who threatened to revoke the Israeli citizenships of Abraham and Szor on Sunday. He called the documentary “shocking” and accused the filmmakers of “betraying the state.”

	“The self-loathing that burns in the creators, who are willing to harm their homeland just to get applause from antisemites around the world, is inconceivable and constitutes a betrayal of the state,” Zohar wrote. “As Minister of Culture, I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for betraying the state.”

schema.headline: Benjamin Netanyahu Calls to ‘Revoke the Citizenship’ of ‘Anyone Who Slanders IDF Soldiers’ Following ‘NAZA’ Documentary Premiere

title: Singer Duncan Sheik Hospitalized, in ‘Critical But Stable Condition’
description: Duncan Sheik, the singer behind hits like the Grammy-nominated “Barely Breathing,” has been hospitalized and is currently receiving medical treatmen
body:
Duncan Sheik, the singer behind hits like the Grammy-nominated “Barely Breathing,” has been hospitalized and is currently receiving medical treatment, per a statement shared on his Instagram page on Wednesday.

	“We would like to share an update with Duncan’s fans and the public,” the statement read. “Duncan is currently receiving medical care and remains in critical but stable condition. Out of respect for Duncan and our family, we will not be sharing any further medical details at this time.”
	

	The statement concluded: “We kindly ask for privacy during this incredibly difficult time and will provide updates when appropriate. Thank you for the continued love and support.”


	According to Sheik’s social media, he has been in and out of the hospital — earlier this month, the singer shared a post with the caption “Sorry for the selfies. But I’m still bored in hospital.” On Aug. 20, he posted a photo with the caption “I would prefer to be home making music. But a bit of reflection is not too bad … boring hospital stays have their benefits (outside the obvious).”

	The news comes ahead of the opening of the new musical “Memoirs of Amorous Gentleman,” an adaptation of Moyoco Anno’s manga graphic novel, for which Sheik penned the score. The first preview is set for September 25, with the opening scheduled for October 15.

	Sheik also composed the music for the Broadway show “Spring Awakening,” a revival of which is set to begin previews off-Broadway this fall. The show first debuted in 2006 and ran for 859 performances, featuring a cast including Lea Michele, Jonathan Groff, Skylar Astin, John Gallagher Jr. and more. It won eight Tony Awards, including Best Musical. “Spring Awakening” was last revived in 2015.

schema.headline: Singer Duncan Sheik Hospitalized, in ‘Critical But Stable Condition’

title: Paul Walter Hauser Explains Mystery Pin He Wore to ‘Resident Evil’ Premiere
description:
Paul Walter Hauser spoke out about the Epstein files with a pin he wore to the “Resident Evil” premiere on Tuesday night in Los Angeles.

	The numbe
body:
Paul Walter Hauser spoke out about the Epstein files with a pin he wore to the “Resident Evil” premiere on Tuesday night in Los Angeles.

	The numbers on the pin affixed to his black T-shirt were the coordinates of the Zorro Ranch in New Mexico. “It was at one point owned by Jeffrey Epstein,” Hauser said. “It’s shrouded in mystery, and then a church supposedly bought it, which is even more disconcerting, I think.”


	The Oscar-nominated actor said he wants “to bring awareness to evil people who are surreptitious and need to have a little Google search done on them.”
	


	In February, Hauser questioned why people in Hollywood weren’t speaking up more for the release of the Epstein files.

	“Dear Hollywood Friends, You spoke up for a great myriad of causes, all worthy, though some more dire than others,” he wrote on Instagram alongside a photo of Macaulay Culkin in “Home Alone.” “Right now, the Epstein files that have been released are implicating lawyers, politicians and members of our entertainment media in the worst crimes one can possibly imagine – the enslavement, r*pe, torture…of children and teenagers. With details and allusions that range from ritual killings to c*nnibalism.”

	“Where are you now? Where are your voices and your hashtags now? Do you fear job loss? Death?” he continued. “Fear God. And protect children. And grow up. I don’t take my Emmy and Golden Globe with me when I die. The U-Haul truck will not follow the hearse in the funeral motorcade.”
	


	In May, NPR reported that New Mexico officials have launched investigations into the ranch, where accusers allege they were abused by Epstein.

	Hauser’s black T-shirt was emblazoned with bright yellow lettering that read, “Kubrick Didn’t Kill Himself.” Hauser told me he was having “fun referencing a little conspiracy theory.”

	Famed director Stanley Kubrick died of a heart attack in his sleep in 1999 at age 70. Conspiracy theorists have claimed that his death was under much more nefarious, but unproven, circumstances.

schema.headline: Paul Walter Hauser Explains Mystery Pin He Wore to ‘Resident Evil’ Premiere

title: ‘Jujutsu Kaisen’ Vaults MAPPA to Anime Studio Lead as Streaming Shifts From Licensing to Ownership, Media Partners Asia Report Finds
description: Anime drew a larger monthly audience than any other genre on Asian streaming platforms between July 2025 and August 2026, and viewing on Netflix gre
body:
Anime drew a larger monthly audience than any other genre on Asian streaming platforms between July 2025 and August 2026, and viewing on Netflix grew nine times faster than the service overall, according to a new report from Media Partners Asia (MPA).

	“The Anime Economy” report draws on ampd audience panels MPA runs across eight Asian markets, on how MPA classifies Netflix’s engagement figures and public filings, and on additional research and interviews MPA conducted. Between 31% and 47% of premium-VOD users across those markets watched anime in any given month during the period, compared with 26% to 34% for the average of the other seven genres tracked. In Japan, the figures ran higher still, from 45% to 59% against 24% to 36%. Anime accounted for 15.6% of tracked premium-VOD hours in the second half of 2025 and 14.0% in the first half of 2026, with the Japan figure at 28%.
	

	“Jujutsu Kaisen” ranked as the top anime title in seven of the eight markets tracked in the first half of 2026, MPA found, propelling MAPPA’s share of regional anime hours from 6.1% in the second half of 2025 to 17.3% in the first half of 2026. That put MAPPA just ahead of TMS Entertainment at 16.6%, with Toei Animation at 13% and titles mastered by Aniplex at 12%.


	Netflix carried roughly half of the region’s anime viewing across the tracking period, holding 51% of anime hours in the second half of 2025 and 50% in the first half of 2026. Japan, the world’s largest anime market, has become a two-way contest between the two biggest global platforms: Prime Video held a 43% share of anime hours there in the second half of 2025, before Netflix pulled even with 42% each in the first half of 2026.
	

	MPA’s classification of Netflix’s “What We Watched” disclosures shows the platform’s Japanese anime viewing climbing from 3.33 billion hours in the first half of 2023 to 4.64 billion hours in the first half of 2026, a 39% jump against 4.5% growth in Netflix’s total viewing over the same period. Anime rose from 3.6% to 4.75% of all Netflix hours in that window. Four-fifths of that viewing remains licensed library content, though MPA points to Netflix’s January 2026 partnership with MAPPA as a marker of the shift toward owned franchises.

	YouTube has become both a marketing channel and a production base for anime: MPA counts 70 million people watching anime-related content there monthly in Japan alone, totaling 2.8 billion hours. Official channels including Aniplex, with 5.1 million monthly viewers, and Toho animation, with 4.8 million, now function as media businesses in their own right, while YouTube-native outfits like Plott are turning out franchises for a fraction of what a traditional TV production would cost.

	MPA counted 21 anime transactions and alliances since 2021, 11 of them struck in 2025 and 2026. Sony took part in seven of those deals, building what MPA calls the industry’s only end-to-end anime operation. Crunchyroll, with 21 million paying subscribers, now sits alongside Sony Pictures, Sony Music and Aniplex within Sony’s portfolio, with the group also holding equity positions in both Kadokawa and Bandai Namco. Toei Animation, Toho, Bandai Namco and other broadcasters have separately bought up studios, distributors and pipelines to build their own capacity.

	MPA projects worldwide anime spending will rise by some 10% annually through 2030, driven mainly by Asia outside Japan and North America, with the gains concentrated among a limited group of franchise-owning companies, studios and platforms. The firm’s base case for the next 24 months is a hybrid financing model in which platforms put up the money for production while studios keep hold of the rights.

	“Anime’s scale is established; the question is where the next growth comes from and who captures it,” said Vivek Couto, CEO and executive director of Media Partners Asia. “The catalysts are streaming pushing deeper into new markets globally, theatrical events on the scale of ‘Infinity Castle’ [“Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba Infinity Castle”] becoming repeatable, and games and merchandise carrying franchises well beyond the screen. The direction is toward ownership: platforms financing production directly, Japanese IP groups buying studios, and the two learning to work together.”
	

	“The constraint is capacity, not demand or capital,” he added. “The studios making the biggest hits are often the least able to invest, and the industry still leans on a handful of franchises. The companies that solve for capacity, and bring the animators with them, will be best placed for the next phase of growth.”

schema.headline: ‘Jujutsu Kaisen’ Vaults MAPPA to Anime Studio Lead as Streaming Shifts From Licensing to Ownership, Media Partners Asia Report Finds

title: Eddie Cahyono’s Busan Competition Title ‘Ibuku,’ Starring Christine Hakim, Boarded by Asian Shadows for World Sales (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Asian Shadows has boarded international sales rights to Eddie Cahyono’s “Ibuku,” starring Christine Hakim and Ayushita Nugraha, which the Busan Inte
body:
Asian Shadows has boarded international sales rights to Eddie Cahyono’s “Ibuku,” starring Christine Hakim and Ayushita Nugraha, which the Busan International Film Festival has selected for its Competition lineup.

	“Ibuku” centers on Sumiati (Hakim), a widow in her 60s isolated in a small Javanese village since her husband took his own life. Her daughter, Sri (Nugraha), had gone abroad for work to get away from an arranged marriage and an abusive spouse. Word reaches Sumiati that Sri now faces execution in Saudi Arabia over the killing of a man who attempted to abuse her, sending the mother on a desperate hunt for the funds to reach her daughter one final time, aided by village chief Djatmiko (Landung Simatupang), who connects her with Indonesian officials and journalists.
	

	Shot on 16mm, the film draws on Cahyono’s research into Indonesian migrant workers, many of whom leave for the city or abroad to escape financial hardship at home, and on the domestic violence and forced marriages some families face in their absence. The story centers on the families left behind, tracing how a mother copes with her daughter’s absence.


	Hakim’s credits span five decades and include “Tjoet Nja’ Dhien,” “Eat Pray Love” and HBO’s “The Last of Us.” Nugraha has appeared in “What They Don’t Talk About When They Talk About Love” and “Kartini: Princess of Java,” while Simatupang’s film work includes “Gie,” “Soegija” and “Kartini: Princess of Java.”

	Indonesia’s ANP Talenta Media, run by Tika Bravani, and Japan’s Knockonwood Inc., headed by Shin Yamaguchi, are producing “Ibuku,” with Hong Kong’s Chinese Shadows executives Isabelle Glachant and Li Xiaorong on board as creative producers. Cahyono holds an executive producer credit via his own Memorieslight Pictures. The film is Bravani’s first as a feature producer.
	

	“‘Ibuku’ is a poetic and touching portrait of a mother through the timeless eyes of her own daughter,” said Maria Ruggieri, Asian Shadows’ head of sales and acquisitions. “We are proud to bring Ibuku to the attention of the International audience.”

	Asian Shadows previously handled sales on Cahyono’s second feature, “Siti” (2014), which won three National Indonesian Awards, for best screenplay, best music and best film, along with prizes at the Singapore International Film Festival and Shanghai International Film Festival. The Hong Kong-based boutique sales company, founded in 2014, represents Asian films by Asian directors, with a roster that has included Mouly Surya’s “Marlina the Murderer in Four Acts” and Garin Nugroho’s “Memories of My Body.”

schema.headline: Eddie Cahyono’s Busan Competition Title ‘Ibuku,’ Starring Christine Hakim, Boarded by Asian Shadows for World Sales (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Bran Flakezz on Winning ‘Unwell Summer Games,’ His Future With Reality TV and the Alex Cooper-Alix Earle Drama
description:
Bran Flakezz is anything but “Unwell.”

	Brandon Edelman, better known as Bran Flakezz online, just emerged as one of four winners of the “Unwell Su
body:
Bran Flakezz is anything but “Unwell.”

	Brandon Edelman, better known as Bran Flakezz online, just emerged as one of four winners of the “Unwell Summer Games” on YouTube, created through Alex Cooper’s “Unwell” network. The four-episode series brought 16 content creators together at a luxury ranch in Canada to compete in a series of challenges for a chance to win a share of $250,000, with the prize money distributed throughout the four days of the competition.
	

	“There’s just so many exciting things happening that sometimes I do have to remind myself to take a step back,” Edelman tells Variety as he gets ready to speak at a Forbes CMO summit in Aspen, Colo.


	Unlike a traditional competition series, “Unwell Summer Games” puts a group of established content creators — many of whom already knew each other — in the same house, ensuring there would be no shortage of drama. In the final episode, the contestants split into four teams for a final challenge. Edelman took home $25,000, alongside Jourdan Riane, Blake Gray and Carly Sutherland Lawrence, the last of whom had a less-than-perfect relationship with Bran on the show.

	“There is a very funny moment where, after we scream at each other, we end up on the same team for the final challenge, and then we proceed to win the show together,” Edelman says, laughing. “Her and I have a very crazy storyline.”

	Edelman got his start posting transparent videos on social media, detailing everything from his life in Philadelphia to the financial realities of being a content creator through his “TikTok Transparency” series. He’s since amassed more than 1 million followers on TikTok and made Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list in Social Media.
	

	After working as a fitting room employee at Forever 21, Edelman went on to compete on Barstool’s “Project Verified” and is now part of Michelle Obama’s Gen Z voter registration intitiative. And after winning the “Unwell Summer Games,” he says he’s just getting started.

	Below, Edelman talks to Variety about his time on “Unwell Summer Games,” his future in reality TV and his take on the Alex Cooper and Alix Earle drama.
	
		Will we see you doing more reality TV after this?	

	Never say never. I think it’s always a case by case situation. As much as I love “Big Brother,” that’s a three-month filming schedule. Three months without posting online for me would be super detrimental, so that would be difficult. I love “Survivor.” No way in hell will you have me on an island like eating rice and sand. I think right now, anything that I want to do in a potential reality TV space is just make something that’s meaningful and real. Something I’ve always noticed when I watch reality TV is that a lot of things feel so overproduced, and that’s not what I want to do. Something that I loved about this show is that none of this drama was manufactured. This truly was how everything played out, and these people’s feelings are very real. That was really refreshing to me.
	
		This isn’t a normal competition show. It’s a house full of content creators. Do you think that having that affected the dynamic and led to some drama?	

	100%. A lot of us had either been friends, met before or, in some circumstances, were exes. These are all people that have a platform, and you’ve probably seen their content. So your first impression of them is, “Oh, I’ve been watching that guy’s videos for three years. He seems like a D-bag online. I wonder how he’s going to be in real life.” I probably had met over half that cast before we walked in there.
	
		Do you still stay in touch with people from the show?	

	Yeah, it’s great. We have a big group chat that’s always popping off, especially right now, because the show is actually airing. We’re all like, “Oh my gosh, you said this in your interview,” or, “Oh my gosh, I can’t believe they put this in that sequence, or they cut this part out.”
	
		Are you watching the drama and thinking, “Oh, I didn’t know she said this”?	

	Definitely. My first reality show [Barstool’s “Project Verified”], I feel like people were talking about me in their interviews, and they probably did talk about me on this show and it just didn’t make the cut. And thank you to the editors for that, because I have a fragile ego. There were definitely some things where I was like, “Oh wow, that person said that about that person. I didn’t realize that.” And even sometimes I will see myself say something and go, “That was kind of mean, Brandon.” But it’s TV, and when you’re in a situation like that, it is a pressure cooker.
	
	
		You became somewhat of a fan favorite while on “Unwell Summer Games.” People online are saying you were the perfect blend of loving drama but still being an empath.	

	They did mention that I was the only person out of all 16 of us that was in a relationship, so my strategy going into it was that I’m going to be a matchmaker. I’m going to help the girls go after the guys that they want. I just wanted to be a safe space for everybody, and have fun.
	
		It was interesting, because you were interested in the drama on the show, but you were never directly involved in any.	

	We all flew out here and we’re working for four days. I didn’t want this to be us all sitting in a circle playing Kumbaya. I definitely wanted there to be realness and honesty. It’s not like I was like, “Everyone needs to fight.” But I was like, ”You want to hook up with that guy? Go for it. This is the time.”
	
		I have to ask about the Blake, Zarah and Carly love triangle. What was it like seeing that unfold in real time?	

	It was complicated, because I liked all three of them so much. You kind of see in my conversation with Zarah that I just wanted her to be very honest with me about her feelings with Blake, and then act on them. My motto in life is always say what you mean and mean what you say, and that’s where I kind of guided her a little bit. And I was like, “If you said this whole time that you really care about Blake and you want to pursue something with him, or your feelings are still there, then it’s one thing to confront Carly, but you have been telling everybody you don’t want any part of this.” I wanted to be a friend for her in that moment, and be like, “Why don’t you take a step back and really reassess?” 

	In Zarah’s defense, though, I do think Carly was a little bit scattered. I was really surprised with Carly, because she was also someone who said she wasn’t going to kiss anybody, and then she goes for Blake. She was obsessed with Chad. Then she goes to Tim. I think it’s complicated when you have someone like Blake who is younger and such a genuine guy. But I think he’s there to have fun and doesn’t necessarily want to be in drama either.
	
		In the finale, there’s a moment where you yell at Carly.	

	Episode 3 ends with me trying to shake Carly and say, “I think a lot of your feelings are valid, but you control how you react to the situation. If you feel like Suede, Zarah and Hallie are excluding you, that’s three out of 16 members of this cast. Maybe you should say, “I’m not vibing with those girls. I’m going to hang out with Brandon, Cassie and Daniela.’” She is playing victim a little bit, and I just wanted her to make the best of this experience and just have fun. This is a silly little show. We leave tomorrow.
	

	One thing they didn’t show me say to her was, “You’re upset that you’re not being picked for anyone’s team, but have you even gone up to any of the captains and say, ‘Hey, I would love to work with you?’ And she’s like, ‘Well, no.’” I said, “You almost expect things to fall on your plate, and when they don’t, you kind of throw your hands up in the air.” It takes two people to communicate. She was just looking at the glass half empty. 

	What you’ll see in the fourth episode is that pressure-cooker moment of me reaching my breaking point because of how she lashed out a little bit on Chad. When people are hurt, they tend to push away the people that they’re closest to, and I think that day Carly was like, “Oh, Bran’s mad at me.” She was talking to everybody else but me, and I wasn’t mad at her. I was just frustrated with her because I loved her so much. I blew a fuse for sure. And it’s not something that I’m proud of. I definitely never want to yell at anybody, let alone a woman.
	
		How does it feel to win a reality show?	

	It feels incredible. One of my favorite “Survivor” players of all time is Cirie Fields, and she did a very infamous speech where she was like, “My mother always said, ‘You may not be able to beat them with these [points to his arms], but you can beat them with this [points to his brain]. And I tied that into my experience. I was like, “I might not beat you in a race, but I will beat you in brain power.”
	
		I have to ask you this. You were just on Alex Cooper’s show. We also saw you at Alix Earle’s “Earle Meets World” premiere. Have you been keeping up with the drama?	

	I will say, I wish we had more fascination with men than we do with women. These are two very successful, powerful women, and everyone just wants to push this narrative of beef and controversy and picking teams. I personally feel like both of them are incredible and super amazing at what they do, and I think one of those elements that both of them have is they’ll never take a business opportunity away from a mutual friend.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: Bran Flakezz on Winning ‘Unwell Summer Games,’ His Future With Reality TV and the Alex Cooper-Alix Earle Drama

Jimmy Buffett
                          Kids Grilled About Mom's Alleged Ketamine Use ...
                          In $275 Million Estate War
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 17, 2026
                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The legal war over Jimmy Buffett's estate is turning ugly … with the late singer's children fielding questions about their mom's alleged drug use ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court docs, obtained by TMZ, Jimmy's son Cameron and daughter Sarah Delaney Buffett, were asked questions about their mom, Jane Buffett, during discovery ... and they were badgered specifically about ketamine and marijuana.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The questions were raised by Jimmy's former financial advisor, Richard Mozenter, as part of the legal battle over control of Jimmy's estate, which is reportedly worth an estimated $275 million.
      

            In court docs, Cameron and Delaney were asked to turn over any documents or communications about Jane's prescription or non-prescription drugs, including but not limited to ketamine and weed, from August 2023 to the present.
      
    
            In their response, the Buffett kids said the request was overboard and said the question sought "harassing documents" that have nothing to do with the case at hand.
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Mozenter sued Jane over the estate, and Jane countersued Richard. In recent docs, Jane claimed Richard was blocking her from viewing accounting records, which she needed to figure out next steps.
      
    
            Jimmy died on September 1, 2023.

title: Nicki Minaj: Issues With ‘Extremely Low’ 'Pink Friday 2' Promo Budget Revealed in Court
description:
Nicki Minaj
                          Issues With ‘Extremely Low’ Budget For 'Pink Friday 2' Prom
body:
Nicki Minaj
                          Issues With ‘Extremely Low’ Budget For 'Pink Friday 2' Promo
                          Revealed in Court Battle
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 17, 2026
                            12:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Nicki Minaj’s team apparently took issue with the budget proposed for promotion for her "Pink Friday 2" album ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            TMZ obtained evidence submitted as part of the ongoing legal battle between 24/7 Productions and Nicki Minaj. The company is suing the rapper and her company, claiming it spent over $275K on hotels and travel under a pre-approved budget but never got reimbursed.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            In an alleged email dated November 29, 2023, a member of Nicki’s team wrote to 24/7 Productions about the scheduled promo. The team member, speaking about the week in New York, wrote “The $250K allowance from Republic [Records] is extremely low. It will cost her at least double that” ... and added that "hotels and transportation alone will eat up the whole amount.”
      

            The email showed the team discussing paying $3K a day for a videographer and photographer for a total of $18K over six days. The team went over paying a seamstress/tailor $700 per day for a total of $4,200 for the same period.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            In regard to flights, the team member asked, “Do we know if her son is going with her? Without her son, her normal plane rider is always over $2K each leg. Plus, she will be in the hotels for many days. I think the $10K rider allowance on the budget is a little low.”
      
    
            The alleged emails are being used to help 24/7 prove its case against Nicki and her company.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As TMZ first reported, 24/7 Productions was hired to coordinate Nicki’s performance at Jingle Ball 2023, for which the entertainer was paid a reported $650K, and a week of promotion for "Pink Friday 2" in New York. The company handles on-site management, travel, staffing, etc.
      
    
            The lawsuit asked for more than $275K in damages. Nicki denied she was personally responsible for the money and asked to be dismissed from the case.
